PROJECT NO. 58481
RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS UNDER
PURA §37.0561
PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
COMMENTS OF THE DIGITAL POWER NETWORK
ON THE STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT OF 16 TAC §25.194

December 19, 2025

Introduction

The Digital Power Network (DPN) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in
response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) Staff Discussion Draft proposing
new 16 TAC §25.194, Large Load Interconnection Standards, under Project No. 58481.
DPN is the largest coalition of Bitcoin miners and digital-infrastructure operators in the
United States, representing more than 85% of publicly traded U.S. Bitcoin mining hashrate
and a rapidly growing footprint of high-density compute facilities across Texas.

Texas is the epicenter of large-load growth in the United States. The state’s competitive
wholesale market, strong transmission build-out, and business-friendly environment have
enabled significant investment in flexible, interruptible loads, including Bitcoin mining and
advanced compute operations, that increasingly support ERCOT’s reliability, demand-
response capabilities, and generation economics. As ERCOT continues to experience
unprecedented industrial load growth, a transparent, predictable, and timely interconnection
framework is essential for both grid operators and market participants.

DPN commends Commission Staff for initiating this rulemaking and for recognizing the need
to modernize interconnection processes for large loads. A clear, well-structured standard
under §25.194 will provide regulatory certainty, reduce delays, and enable Texas to
continue leading the nation in innovative, grid-aligned digital infrastructure development.

We offer the following comments to (1) ensure that the proposed rules appropriately
distinguish between flexible and inflexible large loads; (2) align interconnection standards
with ERCOT’s operational realities; and (3) support a durable, investment-friendly framework
that enhances reliability and protects ratepayers while allowing Texas to remain globally
competitive.
 COMMENTS ON §25.194(a) – Purpose and Scope

DPN supports the Commission’s effort to establish clear, predictable, and transparent
standards for large load interconnections under PURA §37.0561. As ERCOT continues to
experience unprecedented industrial load growth, a modernized framework is essential to
providing regulatory certainty for interconnecting utilities, ERCOT, and large flexible loads.

DPN recommends that the purpose statement explicitly recognize the need for timely
processing and the operational differences between traditional industrial loads and flexible,
interruptible loads, including high-density compute, data centers, and other digital
infrastructure facilities. Incorporating this distinction strengthens alignment with ERCOT
planning practices and supports the Commission’s reliability objectives.

Suggested Revision:
Add the following sentence to subsection (a):

“These standards are intended to support transparent and timely interconnection processes
and to recognize operational distinctions between flexible, interruptible loads and traditional
industrial loads, while ensuring consistency with ERCOT protocols and planning
requirements.”

COMMENTS ON §25.194(b) – Definitions

1. Backup Generating Facilities
The proposed requirement that backup facilities serve at least 50% of contracted peak
demand may inadvertently restrict the use of diverse reliability configurations and does not
reflect operational practices of flexible digital loads. Many facilities rely on interruptibility,
load shedding, or participation in demand-response programs rather than extensive backup
generation.

Recommendation: Define backup generation by function rather than by a fixed percentage,
or provide a range with utility discretion.

Suggested revision: “Generation facilities that support on-site reliability needs and are not
capable of exporting energy to the ERCOT system.”

2. Contracted Peak Demand
The definition ties contracted demand strictly to a securitized agreement and does not
account for phased or modular development, which is standard for digital infrastructure and
other large loads.

Recommendation: Clarify that contracted demand may be phased or milestone-based.
 Suggested revision: “Contracted peak demand may include phased or milestone-based load
schedules.”

3. Discretionary Services Agreement
The sequencing requirements (execution after completion of the interconnection study but
before submission to ERCOT) may introduce procedural rigidity and delay.

Recommendation: Provide flexibility around sequencing and focus on substantive
requirements rather than timing alone.

4. End-Use Customer
Identifying the end-use customer early in the interconnection process may not always be
feasible for developer-led projects.

Recommendation: Allow identification at a later stage if adequate safeguards exist.

5. Interconnecting Electric Utility
No recommended changes.

6. Intermediate Agreement
Rigid sequencing may not match how ERCOT or utilities manage staged studies and
agreements.

Recommendation: Clarify that intermediate agreements apply where required based on
ERCOT study outcomes.

7. Large Load Customer Threshold (75 MW)
The proposed 75 MW threshold is significantly higher than ERCOT’s large-load study trigger
of 25 MW. This may exclude many impactful loads, reduce transparency, and result in
inconsistent treatment across utilities.

Recommendation: Align threshold with ERCOT’s 25 MW standard, or adopt a 50 MW
threshold to capture the majority of high-impact load additions.

Suggested language:
“ERCOT currently conducts large load studies beginning at 25 MW. Aligning the definition
with existing ERCOT practices promotes consistency, avoids unintended incentives to
segment projects, and ensures the rule effectively identifies loads requiring study.”

8. Large Load Interconnection Study
Recommend referencing specific ERCOT Protocol and Planning Guide sections for clarity.
 10. Project Developer
Developer-led projects are common and should be treated as valid applicants.

11. Requested Peak Demand
The definition should explicitly allow phased or incremental requests.

Suggested revision:
“Requested peak demand may be expressed as a phased, incremental, or modular forecast
where appropriate.”

DPN COMMENTS ON §25.194(c) (Disclosures and Study Fee Requirements)

General Comment on §25.194(c)
This subsection establishes the prerequisites for entering the ERCOT large-load study
process. DPN supports the Commission’s goal of ensuring that projects entering the queue
demonstrate baseline readiness, but several provisions, in their current form, may
unintentionally discourage investment, create unnecessary administrative burdens, or
introduce duplicative disclosure obligations that are not aligned with ERCOT’s existing
processes.

We recommend refining these requirements to ensure transparency without compromising
customer confidentiality, market competitiveness, or development flexibility.

(1) Developer vs. End-Use Customer Disclosure

DPN Concern
This disclosure itself is reasonable, but later provisions in the rule appear to treat developer-
initiated requests with added scrutiny or requirements. Developer-led interconnection is
extremely common in Texas and a major driver of economic development.

Recommendation
Clarify that developer-initiated requests are fully valid participants in the interconnection
process and should not face additional barriers.

(2) Site Control Requirements

DPN Concern
Requiring a deed, executed lease, or binding option at the time of study initiation may be too
rigid and out of sync with how phased or speculative energy-intensive development occurs.
 Economic development projects often require transmission feasibility before committing to a
lease or land acquisition. This requirement could push projects toward premature land
control, increasing risk and discouraging investment.

Recommendation
Allow conditional or provisional site control documents, such as:
    • Letter of intent
    • Conditional purchase/lease agreements
    • Escrowed site option
    • Executed MOU with landowner

Suggested revision:
“A customer may demonstrate site control through legally binding or conditionally binding
instruments sufficient to show control upon successful interconnection study outcomes.”
This maintains integrity while reducing unreasonable upfront burdens.

(3) Substantially Similar Interconnection Request

DPN Concern
The rule requires the customer to disclose whether it is pursuing similar interconnection
requests elsewhere, a requirement no other ERCOT process currently imposes. This raises
concerns:
   • It introduces subjective interpretation of “substantially similar.”
   • It creates competitive sensitivity risks, even with anonymization.
   • It may be impossible for large companies with multiple divisions or developers with
       multiple active sites to determine what is "material."
   • It could deter flexible-load developers who evaluate multiple sites in parallel, which is
       normal and efficient.

Recommendation
(a) Remove the requirement entirely, or
(b) Greatly narrow the scope to apply only when:
    • multiple requests share the exact same end-use customer,
    • with the same load characteristics, and
    • where duplicative reservations could artificially distort system planning.

If retained, the Commission must define “substantially similar” objectively to avoid future
disputes.

Specific Recommended Revisions
   1. Define “substantially similar interconnection request” narrowly and objectively.
   2. Limit disclosure to materially duplicative requests for the same project.
    3. Explicitly protect commercially sensitive information.

(4) Phased Energization Schedule Disclosure

DPN Concern
This requirement is appropriate in principle but should account for:
    • uncertainty in long-term modular construction
    • changes in ramp schedules due to market economics
    • the fact that high-density flexible loads often energize in variable increments

Recommendation
Allow ranges or approximate timelines at initial submission.

Suggested revision:
“A customer may submit approximate or range-based energization schedules, with updates
provided as material changes occur.”

(5) Backup Generating Facilities Disclosure

DPN Concern
Backup generation data should be disclosed only to the extent it affects interconnection or
reliability modeling. The full list of characteristics (fuel source, start time, nameplate
capacity) may be excessive for many facilities and create confidentiality concerns.
Also, backup generation is not always in place at early project stages.

Recommendation
   • Allow disclosure of backup generation if used for operational reliability, not force
     early-stage commitments.
   • Clarify that disclosure is required only if backup generation materially affects load
     modeling.
   • Reinforce confidentiality protections.

Suggested revision:
“A customer must disclose planned backup generation to the extent that such resources
materially affect load modeling or system impact studies.”

(6) Dynamic Modeling Requirement

DPN Concern
Dynamic load models are often not available early in project development. Requiring them
before conducting a study may delay queue entry and contradict the Commission’s goal of
accelerating interconnection.
 Recommendation
   • Allow submission of a standard or generic model at the outset.
   • Allow updated models later as equipment decisions finalize.

Suggested revision:
“Customers may submit preliminary or generic dynamic models if final equipment
specifications are unavailable at the time of study initiation.”

(7) Study Fee Structure

DPN Concern
The fee schedule must be:
   • transparent,
   • predictable, and
   • proportionate to actual study complexity.

As written, the rule:
   • sets high minimum fees, but DPN recognizes this is a tactic for minimizing the
        number of phantom load requests,
   • allows unlimited upward cost exposure,
   • does not guarantee utilities’ reasonableness or consistency,
   • could create barriers for smaller flexible loads.

Recommendations
   1. Require justification for fees exceeding the minimum.
   2. Ensure cost caps or proportionality tied to actual study scope.
   3. Require ERCOT and utilities to publish annual fee methodologies.
   4. Permit refunds for overcollection or unused study time.

Suggested revision language:
“Study fees above the minimum thresholds should be based on demonstrable, project-
specific incremental study costs and supported by transparent methodologies.”

DPN COMMENTS ON §25.194(d) - Large Load Interconnection Study

(d) — Timing + Study Initiation

DPN Concern
The rule requires utilities to begin studies within 30 days after receiving disclosures,
financial commitments, and study fees. This is generally positive—but the front-loaded
document requirements are so extensive that they may delay the actual start date or lead to
disputes about “complete” applications.
 DPN Recommendation
Clarify that utilities must begin the study based on materially complete information, not
perfect completeness.

Suggested language:
“The 30-day window should commence once the utility determines the submission is
materially complete based on ERCOT study requirements.”

(d)(1) — 5-Day Notification for Any Change

DPN Concern
Requiring notice within 5 days for any change to disclosed information is unrealistic and
administratively burdensome. Large flexible loads commonly refine schedules, engineering
data, and equipment specs during development.
This rule risks:
    • excessive reporting;
    • inconsistent compliance;
    • unnecessary friction between utilities and customers.

DPN Recommendation
Limit updates to only material changes, aligned with ERCOT definitions.

Suggested revision:
“Customers must provide notification within 10 business days of any material change that
affects load characteristics or interconnection requirements.”

(d)(2) — Additional Study Fee for Requesting More Capacity

DPN Concern
The rule forces customers to pay additional study fees if they seek additional MW, or
withdraw within 10 days. Problems:
    • 10 days is too short for large capital decision-making
    • study-fee exposure is unbounded
    • flexible loads often scale modularly; this is normal, not speculative

This provision penalizes phased and modular development, which is central to ERCOT’s
ecosystem.

DPN Recommendation
  • Allow scaled increases up to a threshold (e.g., 10% or 20%) without triggering a full
     new fee
    •   Allow 30–45 days to evaluate new cost exposure
   •   Require utilities to justify cost increases with transparent methodologies

Suggested revision:
“Modest increases (e.g., up to 20%) in requested peak demand should not trigger a new
study fee, provided they do not materially alter network upgrade requirements.”

(d)(3) — Notice of Study Completion
No issues, but we recommend adding explicit transparency requirements.

DPN COMMENTS ON §25.194(e) - Discretionary Services Agreement (DSA)
This subsection imposes excessive, duplicative, and, at times, commercially invasive
requirements that go well beyond normal ERCOT practice or interconnection norms in
competitive markets.

We recommend targeted fixes to prevent bottlenecks and protect customer confidentiality
while maintaining ERCOT’s planning needs.

(e)(1) Developer vs. End-Use Customer

DPN Concern
Neutral requirement, but the rule later attaches heavier burdens to developers, not end-
users.

DPN Recommendation
Explicitly state that developer-led interconnection requests are fully valid and should not be
disadvantaged.

(e)(2) Site Control — Minimum 50% Duration Rule

DPN Concern
The requirement that site control must cover 50% of the expected time to reach peak
demand is arbitrary and unworkable.

Problems:
   • disconnects from ERCOT timelines
   • may require 5–10 year lease commitments before feasibility is known
   • discourages early-stage site development
   • inconsistent with Texas’ economic-development model
 DPN Recommendation
Allow conditional site control instruments, including pre-development agreements, options,
or letters of intent.

Suggested revision:
“Site control must be sufficient to demonstrate the ability to construct and operate the
project upon successful completion of interconnection studies.”

(e)(3) — Substantially Similar Interconnection Request (again)
This repeats the problematic Section (c)(3) requirement.

DPN Concern
Duplicative and overly burdensome, with major confidentiality and competition risks.

DPN Recommendation
Strongly recommend removing or significantly narrowing the requirement.

If retained, limit disclosure only to:
     • duplicative requests for the same customer at the same site, or
     • situations where a customer has already executed multiple contracts for the same
         load.

Suggest defining “substantially similar” objectively.

(e)(4) Site-Related Studies + Attestation

DPN Concern
This requirement intrudes far beyond the scope of electric interconnection. Forcing utilities
to police water, wastewater, and gas development progress is not aligned with ERCOT’s
jurisdiction and creates:
    • legal risk
    • administrative burdens
    • unnecessary delays
    • privacy issues
    • overreach into local permitting processes

The required officer attestation is extreme.
DPN Recommendation
Strike or significantly narrow.

Suggested revision:
 “Customers should affirm they are pursuing necessary site-related studies to support project
development, without mandating reporting of specific non-electric utility workstreams.”

(e)(5) State and Local Regulatory Approvals + Attestation

DPN Concern
Similar issues:
   • electric utilities are not responsible for validating non-electric permitting
   • developers often pursue permits in parallel, not sequentially
   • requiring updates “when requested” creates unlimited reporting burdens
   • officer-level attestation is unnecessary and exposes customers to liability

DPN Recommendation
Replace with a simplified requirement:
“Customers must demonstrate that they are pursuing required state and local permits prior
to energization.”

No attestation required.

(e)(6) Phased Energization Schedule
Same concerns as before:
    • early-stage projects cannot provide precise dates
    • modular loads energize in flexible patterns
    • requiring MW and MVAr may not be possible until equipment selection is final

DPN Recommendation
Allow approximate or preliminary ranges.

(e)(7) Backup Generating Facilities
Repeats the same issue as Section (c)(5).

DPN Recommendation
Require only what is needed for load modeling. Remove detailed operational disclosures.

(e)(8) Financial Security — $50,000/MW

DPN Concern
This is one of the most consequential and problematic provisions in the draft.
Problems:
    • $50,000/MW security is extremely high
    • Applies to contracted peak demand, even for multi-phase, multi-year buildouts
    • Disadvantages flexible loads (miners, HPC) relative to traditional heavy industry
    •   Creates significant capital barriers
   •   Far exceeds practices in other jurisdictions
   •   Could create a chilling effect on development in Texas

For a 200 MW project:
→ Required security = $10,000,000

This essentially becomes a massive upfront collateral requirement before construction
begins.

DPN Recommendation
Suggested alternatives:

Option A – Phase security with energization milestones
Customers provide security only for the phase being energized, not full buildout.

Option B – Reduce security to $10,000–$20,000 per MW
Aligned with PJM, MISO, SPP practices.

Option C – Cap total security amounts
Avoid unlimited exposure for mega-projects.

Option D – Allow broader forms of credit assurance
Many high-growth digital infrastructure companies do not have BBB credit ratings.
Security should be proportional to actual upgrade costs and phased over the project
development timeline. DPN recommends a lower per-MW requirement and flexibility in
acceptable forms of financial security.

§25.194(f) – Submission of Study to ERCOT / Automatic Cancellation

DPN Concerns
  • 30 days to execute a DSA after study completion is tight for large, capital-intensive
     projects that may require internal approvals, financing decisions, or negotiation of
     terms based on the study results.
  • Automatic cancellation with no option for extension, even if both the customer and
     utility want to proceed, creates unnecessary churn and queue risk.

DPN Recommendations
  1. Allow extensions by mutual agreement between the utility and customer.
  2. Clarify that the utility must provide a complete draft DSA promptly after study
     completion so the 30-day clock isn’t eaten up by utility delay.
 §25.194(g) – Notification of Additional Study

DPN Positives
  • Requiring ERCOT to state why additional study is needed and provide a timeline
     estimate is good transparency.
  • Requiring the utility to share ERCOT communications with the customer is also good.

DPN Concerns
  • 10 days to commit to additional study costs is too short for large-load customers who
     may need to:
        o review revised cost/risk;
        o brief management/boards;
        o coordinate multiple sites or options.
  • Study-fee exposure is unbounded.
  • There is no standard of reasonableness for the additional study costs or a
     requirement for a cost breakdown.

DPN Recommendations
  1. Extend the decision window to 30 days or at least 20 business days.
  2. Require that additional study costs be itemized and reasonably related to the
     incremental study scope.
  3. Allow scaled increases up to a threshold (e.g., 10% or 20%) without triggering a full
     new fee.
  4. Clarify that failure to pay is treated as withdrawal only for that specific request, not
     other interconnection efforts by the same customer.

§25.194(h) – Intermediate Agreement & Financial Obligations

(e)(2) Site Control — Minimum 50% Duration Rule

DPN Concern
The requirement that site control must cover 50% of the expected time to reach peak
demand is arbitrary and unworkable.

Problem
    • Disconnects from ERCOT timelines
    • May require 5–10 year lease commitments before feasibility is known
    • Discourages early-stage site development
    • Inconsistent with Texas’ economic-development model
DPN Recommendation
Allow conditional site-control instruments, including pre-development agreements, options,
or letters of intent.
 Suggested Revision
“Site control must be sufficient to demonstrate the ability to construct and operate the
project upon successful completion of interconnection studies.”

(e)(3) Substantially Similar Interconnection Requests (Again)
This subsection repeats the problematic requirement in Section (c)(3).

DPN Concern
Duplicative and overly burdensome, creating significant confidentiality and competition
risks.

DPN Recommendation
Remove or significantly narrow the requirement.

If retained, disclosure should be limited only to:
     • Duplicative requests for the same customer at the same site; or
     • Situations where a customer has executed multiple contracts for the same load.

Further, “substantially similar” should be defined using clear, objective criteria.

(h) 180-Day Deadline for Intermediate Agreement

Concern
   • A 180-day deadline is often insufficient for major projects that depend on:
         o Local zoning and permitting outcomes
         o Financing and investor timelines
         o Offtake or tenant negotiations
   • Automatic cancellation with no flexibility will eliminate serious projects that are
      progressing but subject to normal development timelines.

Recommendation
   • Allow extensions by mutual agreement.
   • Permit projects to maintain queue position by demonstrating meaningful progress
     (e.g., permits filed, financing underway, design milestones met) rather than imposing
     a rigid 180-day deadline.

(h)(1) Developer vs. End-Use Customer — Contract Requirement
Concern
    • Requiring a signed end-use contract at this stage is unrealistic for many development
       models.
    •   Data centers, campuses, and industrial parks often finalize tenants only after
       interconnection certainty improves.

Recommendation
   • Allow disclosure of:
         o Whether a customer is identified;
         o Whether an LOI or MOU exists; or
         o Whether the project will operate on a merchant basis.
   • Do not require a signed contract as a condition to proceed.

(h)(2) Site Control Through Peak Year

Concern
   • Effectively forces long-term site commitments (often 10+ years) before key project
      decision points.
   • Out of step with commercial leasing practices and phased build-out models.

Recommendation
   • Replace with a standard requiring site control sufficient to cover construction and
     initial operations.
   • Allow flexibility for longer-term arrangements to be finalized later.
   • Avoid hard linkage to the “year contracted peak demand is expected to be reached,”
     which may change over time.

(h)(3) Substantially Similar Interconnection Requests

Concern
This is the third repetition of the same obligation and continues to suffer from:
    • Vague definitions
    • Confidentiality risks
    • Penalization of firms evaluating multiple potential sites

Recommendation
   • Remove or narrowly tailor the requirement as previously discussed.
   • Cross-reference earlier comments to avoid redundancy.

(h)(4) & (h)(5) Site Studies, State/Local Approvals, and Officer Attestations

Concerns
   • Overreach into local development and non-electric regulatory jurisdictions.
   • Makes utilities de facto monitors of land use and permitting.
   • Exposes customers to unnecessary legal risk and ongoing reporting burdens.
    •   Not required for ERCOT reliability or transmission planning.

Recommendations
   • Replace with a high-level certification that the customer is responsible for obtaining
     non-electric permits prior to energization.
   • Remove officer attestations and recurring reporting requirements.

(h)(6) & (h)(7) Schedule and Backup Generation
These subsections raise the same issues addressed in subsections (c) and (e):
    • Schedule: Allow approximate or milestone-based timelines rather than precise
       month/year commitments far in advance.
    • Backup generation: Limit required information to what is necessary for system
       modeling, not detailed operational strategies.

(h)(8) Financial Security for Significant Equipment and Services

Concern
This requirement is additive to:
    • The $50,000/MW security in subsection (e)(8); and
    • The full CIAC payment in subsection (h)(9).

Taken together, these provisions impose substantial upfront collateral and capital burdens
on large flexible loads — particularly Bitcoin miners and AI/HPC operators — who:
    • May be unrated or below investment grade;
    • Are often high-growth and equity-financed.

Additionally, allowing security based on “expected costs” without caps or cost-
reasonableness standards grants utilities excessive discretion.

Recommendations
   • Limit security for long-lead equipment to a portion (e.g., 25–50%) of projected costs.
   • Allow security to be phased as procurement milestones are met.
   • Expand acceptable forms of security beyond investment-grade entities (e.g., audited
     unrated entities, performance bonds, escrow arrangements).

(h)(9) Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC)

Overview
This provision:
    • Requires CIAC equal to expected interconnection costs directly attributable to the
       customer.
    •   Explicitly includes new lines, substation upgrades, and system upgrades that “would
       not be required but for” the customer.
   •   Requires cost pro-ration among multiple large-load customers and credits earlier
       customers when later customers interconnect.

Concerns
   • Lack of transparency and dispute resolution regarding:
         o How “would not be required but for” determinations are made;
         o How costs are allocated among multiple customers;
         o How CIAC credits are tracked and returned.
   • When combined with security requirements, total upfront exposure becomes
      excessive.

Recommendations
   • Require utilities to provide detailed cost breakdowns and CIAC allocation
     methodologies.
   • Establish clear dispute-resolution processes, including PUCT review, for contested
     allocations.
   • Clarify that CIAC payments are not duplicative of other charges or security already
     posted for the same assets.


§25.194(i) Withdrawal of Requested or Contracted Load

DPN Position
DPN supports the concept of allowing customers to withdraw part or all of their requested
megawatts but recommends targeted refinements.

Allowing withdrawal is reasonable and consistent with standard interconnection practice.

However, the rule lacks clarity regarding what costs are considered “outstanding” and
exposes customers to unpredictable and uncapped cost liability.

Key Concerns
   1. Unlimited cost exposure
      The phrase “costs incurred … that cannot be canceled” is undefined and could be
      interpreted broadly by utilities. Without cost caps or transparency, customers face
      unpredictable financial exposure.
   2. No requirement for itemized accounting
      The rule does not require utilities to provide detailed, auditable documentation of
      outstanding costs before drawing on posted security.
    3. CIAC is non-refundable in all circumstances
      Even where no construction has occurred or where subsequent ERCOT restudies
      show upgrades are unnecessary, CIAC is automatically unrecoverable. This approach
      is punitive and inconsistent with cost-causation principles.

DPN Recommendations
  • Require a detailed, itemized accounting of all “outstanding amounts owed.”
  • Clarify that only costs actually incurred and non-recoverable may be drawn from
     security.
  • Allow partial CIAC refunds if no construction has begun or if system needs change.
  • Require utilities to mitigate costs to the extent reasonably possible.



§25.194(j) Reallocation of Capacity
This subsection is among the most problematic provisions in the rule.

What the Rule Does
  • If a large-load customer misses a milestone by 18 months, the utility must reallocate
      the customer’s capacity.
  • The utility refunds remaining security only after receiving security from a replacement
      customer.
  • Outstanding costs are drawn first, raising the same concerns identified in subsection
      (i).

Major DPN Concerns

   1. The 18-month milestone trigger is overly rigid
      Flexible loads, including Bitcoin miners and AI/HPC operators, commonly scale in
      phases. Development timelines shift due to market conditions, equipment
      availability, and supply-chain constraints. An 18-month deadline is arbitrary and not
      tied to ERCOT operational needs.
   2. Automatic reallocation penalizes flexible loads
      Loads intentionally designed to be interruptible and reliability-supportive should not
      be treated as speculative or inactive simply because growth is modular or non-linear.
   3. Reallocation depends on the existence of a replacement customer
      If no new customer exists, the original customer’s capital may be held indefinitely,
      creating unacceptable financial uncertainty.

   4. No dispute-resolution process
      The rule does not identify who determines whether a milestone was “missed” or
      whether delays were reasonable or outside the customer’s control.
    5. No requirement for utilities to mitigate costs
      Utilities could procure equipment prematurely, unnecessarily increasing customer
      liability.

DPN Recommendations

A. Replace rigid cancellation/reallocation with a progress-based standard
Rather than a strict 18-month deadline, allow customers to demonstrate:
    • Construction progress;
    • Procurement progress; or
    • Documented delays outside the customer’s control (e.g., permitting or supply-chain
       constraints).

B. Require utilities to offer extensions for good cause
Extensions are routinely granted in other ERCOT planning contexts and should be available
here.

C. Protect customers against indefinite security holds
Refunds should occur even if a replacement customer does not immediately exist, subject to
recovery of documented, non-recoverable costs.

D. Define milestone requirements in ERCOT protocols
Milestones should be standardized through ERCOT protocols, not left to utility discretion, to
ensure consistency across service territories.

§25.194(k) Terms for Refund of Financial Security After Energization
This subsection establishes an extremely slow and rigid refund schedule.

What the Rule Requires
  • A refund of 20% of remaining security at energization;
  • Additional refunds ratably as milestones are met;
  • Final refund only after the load sustains operations at contracted peak demand for
      five consecutive years.

DPN Concerns
  1. Refunds are tied to contracted peak demand, not actual operations
     Flexible loads rarely operate at 100% of contracted peak demand and typically scale
     modularly.

   2. The five-year requirement is excessive and unnecessary
      This structure:
          o Ties up capital for years;
           o    Fails to reflect changing growth trajectories; and
          o    Is not required to support ERCOT reliability.
   3. The refund structure penalizes flexible operations
      Flexible loads may intentionally reduce consumption in response to market
      conditions, demand response programs, or ancillary services participation. The rule
      penalizes this behavior.
   4. The refund schedule is overly back-loaded
      Utilities face limited ongoing risk once interconnection upgrades are constructed, yet
      customers bear prolonged financial exposure.

DPN Recommendations

A. Tie refunds to construction and energization milestones, not peak demand
Allow staged refunds when:
    • Interconnection assets are installed;
    • Energization occurs; and
    • The customer meets agreed-upon minimum load thresholds.

B. Remove or substantially shorten the five-year requirement
Reduce the final hold period to no more than two years.

C. Allow refund upon commercial operation at initial energization levels
Do not require full contracted peak demand to trigger refunds.

D. Require transparency in withheld amounts
Utilities should provide itemized explanations of any retained security to support cost
recovery.

§25.194(l) ERCOT Operational Standards

Overall DPN Position
DPN supports ERCOT establishing operational standards through market protocols rather
than through ad hoc utility requirements. However, ERCOT’s proposed voltage ride through
(VRT) framework, if approved, could create significant regulatory uncertainty for already
operating and prospective large loads.

Key Clarifications Needed
   1. ERCOT operational standards must be non-discriminatory among flexible loads,
       industrial loads, and traditional customers.
   2. Standards should be adopted through the formal stakeholder process (PRS, TAC, and
       ERCOT Board), not through unilateral action.
    3. Standards must recognize that flexible loads provide reliability benefits and should
      not be regulated as inflexible industrial loads.
   4. ERCOT should provide clear, quantifiable reasoning for the reliability benefits from
      the proposed VRT framework.

DPN Recommendation
Include language ensuring ERCOT standards are:
    • Developed through the formal Nodal Protocol Revision Request (NPRR) process;
    • Applied consistently across customer classes; and
    • Respectful of the operational characteristics of flexible, interruptible loads.
Ensure that the proposed VRT requirements are
    • Transparent and evidence-based.
    • Applied primarily on a prospective basis with technologically feasible and practicable
       paths for existing facilities.
    • Narrowly tailored to specific, demonstrable reliability risks so that Texas can maintain
       both a stable, reliable grid and a predictable regulatory environment for continued
       investment and growth.
 Responses to Commission Staff Questions on Proposed §25.194

1. Should the Commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
customer is pursuing a “substantially similar” interconnection request?

DPN Response:
Yes, if the requirement is retained, the Commission should define narrow, objective
parameters. Absent clear standards, the concept of “substantially similar” is vague,
inconsistently applied, and creates confidentiality and competition risks without
corresponding reliability benefits.

Recommended Parameters (if retained):
A request should be deemed “substantially similar” only where all of the following apply:
    • The requests are submitted by the same customer or affiliated entity;
    • The requests are for the same physical site or point of interconnection (or sites within
       a clearly defined, limited geographic radius); and
    • The requests seek to serve the same underlying load, rather than alternative
       development options or phased project concepts.

Requests should not be considered substantially similar merely because they:
   • Are located within the same load zone or transmission region;
   • Reflect different development scenarios, phased build-outs, or alternative sites under
      evaluation; or
   • Represent contingency planning common to large infrastructure development.

2. Should the Commission specify what is and is not competitively sensitive information
for purposes of disclosures under subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3)?

DPN Response:
If the Commission retains these disclosure provisions, it should clearly delineate what
information is and is not competitively sensitive to prevent over-disclosure and protect
legitimate commercial interests.

Information That Should Not Be Considered Competitively Sensitive (and may be
disclosed):
    • ERCOT load zone or general transmission region;
    • Whether the customer has submitted multiple requests under evaluation;
    • Whether requests relate to the same customer or affiliated entities (without naming
       counterparties);
    • General project status (e.g., active, withdrawn, paused).
 Information That Should Be Considered Competitively Sensitive (and may be anonymized
or withheld):
    • Specific site addresses or parcel-level location data;
    • Customer identity, tenant identity, or offtake counterparties;
    • Contractual terms, pricing, or load profiles;
    • Phasing schedules, ramp curves, or commercial strategies;
    • Financing arrangements or investor participation.

ERCOT and utilities can identify duplicative or non-viable requests using objective identifiers
without disclosure of commercially sensitive business information.

3. Should customers be required to notify utilities and ERCOT of any change to disclosed
information, or only material changes?

DPN Response:
Customers should be required to notify utilities and ERCOT only of material changes, not all
changes.

Requiring continuous updates for immaterial or routine project evolution would create
unnecessary administrative burden and discourage early-stage development without
providing reliability benefits.

Recommended Definition of “Material Change”:
A material change should be limited to changes that:
   • Affect the point of interconnection;
   • Result in a material increase or decrease in total requested MW (e.g., ≥20%);
   • Reflect a change in customer control or withdrawal of the project; or
   • Would reasonably require ERCOT or the utility to re-run system impact studies.

Changes to development timelines, tenant negotiations, internal financing arrangements, or
phased build-out strategies should not be deemed material.

4. Should the Commission standardize the rate of refund for financial security under
subsection (k)(1)?

DPN Response:
Yes, but the refund structure should be standardized around project execution milestones,
not fixed operational timelines or sustained peak demand.

A rigid, time-based refund (e.g., 20% per year) would continue to disadvantage flexible and
modular loads and does not align with actual utility risk.
 Recommended Standardized Refund Framework:
   • At energization: Refund a meaningful portion of remaining security (e.g., ≥30–40%),
     reflecting that interconnection assets are installed and utility risk materially declines.
   • Post-energization milestones: Additional staged refunds tied to:
         o Completion of interconnection facilities;
         o Commercial operation at initial energization levels;
         o Demonstrated ongoing cost recovery for utility investments.
   • Final hold period: No more than two years, regardless of whether full contracted peak
     demand is reached.

Refunds should not be conditioned on sustained operation at 100% of contracted peak
demand, which is inconsistent with the operational reality of flexible loads.

5. Are changes to other Commission rules necessary to align with this rulemaking?

DPN Response:
Yes. To ensure consistency and avoid conflicting obligations, the Commission should review
and align the following areas:
   • PUCT interconnection and CIAC rules:
       Clarify cost-causation standards, refund eligibility, and non-duplication of security
       requirements across rules.
   • ERCOT Protocols:
       Ensure that milestone definitions, progress standards, and operational obligations
       are addressed through the stakeholder-driven NPRR process, not through utility-
       specific interpretations of Commission rules.
   • Large load and data center-related rules or guidance:
       Confirm consistent treatment of flexible, interruptible loads across demand
       response, reliability, and planning frameworks.

Without alignment, customers may face overlapping, inconsistent, or duplicative obligations
that increase cost without improving reliability.
